text: Prompt engineering is described consistently as designing instructions to guide a model without altering its parameters, and as a form of programming that customizes outputs and interactions.

Prompt engineering is also described as poorly consolidated: it is said to have conflicting terminology, to be treated as empirical and ad hoc without a standardized theoretical framework, and to be a critical yet loosely defined skill.

Several sources describe a movement beyond prompts: one survey frames it as a shift from input-level linguistic control to system-level contextual orchestration, and the externalization review places the harness at a stage extending into persistent infrastructure.

The sources agree on the direction of the boundary but phrase it differently. Prompt engineering changes instructions, context engineering changes the evidence presented, and harness engineering takes the operating environment as its object of analysis. The externalization review separately calls the harness a structured form of context engineering, so the boundary between context engineering and harness is not drawn identically.

Components are attributed across the stages: context adaptation and evolving playbooks, memory as a file system accessed through tool calls, tool schemas that consume context budget, orchestration roles separating planning, generation and evaluation, and verification as a harness component.

Evaluation evidence converges on the claim that the harness matters: changing the execution system around a fixed model can alter performance and reverse rankings, and a reported score reflects a model–harness–environment configuration.

Sources diverge on where capability ends up. One survey proposes that routine support moves into model weights while governance stays external, and another says the loop is both internalized into weights and externalized into skills and harnesses.

The literature articulates a progression from prompt-level instruction design, to context-level management of what the model sees, to harness-level treatment of the surrounding execution environment, though the exact boundaries are phrased differently across sources.
Memory, tool use, orchestration and verification are attributed mainly to the system-level and harness stages, but these claims do not show a single agreed assignment of components to stages.

Some of the empirical support is limited: one context-compression experiment used a synthetic task with a single model and budget, and the context-rot hypothesis is stated as untested by prior published studies.
The claims do not settle whether capability will mainly move into weights or into external harnesses.
Test the context-rot and tool-attrition hypothesis directly, since it is described as untested.
Repeat context-management comparisons with multiple models and budgets on non-synthetic tasks, because the existing experiment is limited to a single model and budget.
Develop shared definitions and a common vocabulary for the three stages, given the terminological fragmentation and the differing placement of the harness relative to context engineering.
Report evaluations as full model–harness–environment configurations and separate the entangled effects, since rankings can reverse.
Study evaluation beyond final task success, including verification under incomplete feedback and the risk that a new verifier accepts underspecified solutions.

The sources describe a split in where agent functions reside: one harness survey proposes that routine capability-bearing support migrates into model weights while constraint-bearing governance functions remain external, and the agent-loop survey likewise argues that the loop is being internalized into weights and externalized into skills and harnesses. Both are proposals or arguments, and the sources do not report an empirical test of which functions migrate.
